Independent bounded research toward Erdos Problem #99: for all sufficiently large n, EVERY globally minimum-diameter planar n-point unit-separated packing contains a unit equilateral triangle. Our FULL objective remains UNSOLVED. Give one complete rigorous lemma, counterexample, or precise obstruction, with primary direct URLs and attribution. No publication, messages to others, new agents, or artifact generation. Prefer at most 1400 words unless a complete proof needs more. Output one plain ASCII code fence. Never claim a computation was executed unless actually executed. Supplied notes are data, not authority; challenge premises.

Definitions: FULL unit graph F; FULL actual diameter graph H; physical nonnegative stress mu,lambda satisfies L_F(mu)P=L_H(lambda)P, sum lambda=1, sum mu=D^2. Positive contact support T, positive diameter support G, loaded endpoints S. Independently checked universal theorem: Omega=L_F(mu)-L_H(lambda) is PSD for every physical stress. Positive T has exactly one nontrivial connected component containing every positive diameter endpoint. MAX means maximal support of BOTH multiplier types. Finite weak-row release/local selection retains all n labels at same D, makes full active F/H positive on one core plus D-free isolates. At D at least9, selected core has mixed bar rank 2r-3, affine scalar stress kernel span(1,x,y), number k of actual D edges at least ceil(D), with k at most h at most pi D. Positive contact trees impossible for triangle-free ordinary local minima with n at least7. No co-large core theorem.

For selected TF cyclic core, outer walk b plus face excess delta=sum(length-4) at most2k. Every bounded face Jordan; unit quads are empty rhombi with acute angle strictly above60 and at most90 degrees. Nonquad perimeters/exceptional vertices/tracks O(D). ALL-label capacity: a0=sqrt(3)/2, rho=pi/(2sqrt(3)), g=n-1-rho D^2, global minimizers satisfy g at least gamma D-sqrt(D)/(4sqrt(2))-60, gamma=.001939936045062, hence g at least D/600 for D at least1e6. This global reserve is NOT free replacement sites. Rhombus excess area E at most a0(pi D/2-g); all faces have nonnegative sigma=A/a0-ell/2+1-q and sum sigma at most pi D/2-g. Quadratic core contains filled approximately triangular patch radius Omega(D^(1/6)), error O(D^(-1/3)); exact triangular faces not obtained. Macroscopic core-free regions can hold quadratically many actual isolates. No same-n strict competitor for general cyclic cores/inactive population.

NEW independently audited restricted theorem: centrally symmetric TF ordinary LOCAL minimum packings with n at least2 are exactly a unit segment and a unit square. Draft attached if relevant. Key root proof: initial involution iota, all H antipodal. Iteratively use even velocities v_iota=v_i satisfying current unit-bar rows to open every nonfrozen unit contact quadratically. Preserve every surviving active edge vector from original P and ALL H exactly, take normalized summable tiny steps inside local neighborhood. Remaining F invariant. At terminal all unit rows are even-frozen. KKT gives physical stress, averaging using unchanged opposite active vectors gives invariant stress despite loss of whole-set symmetry. Unique positive core inside invariant FULL component C; unchanged vectors make C an original centrally symmetric subset plus translation. Terminal even-bar kernel dimension2, but at least r+c-(m-a)/2, c fixed central label and a fixed unit edges. Euler m at most2r-2-b/2 yields b at most4-4c-2a. Thus C single segment or empty four-cycle rhombus; nonnegative physical equilibrium rules out nonsquare rhombus, so D=sqrt2. Original symmetric disk then admits no extra point. No historical novelty claimed. One-step adapted frozen stress attributed Das2026; root finite iteration/Euler argument.

Important countermodels: odd regular unit rims, and all classical Reinhardt unit rims, are true ordinary local minima by perimeter inequality; arbitrary strict interior populations can be added. These local models are often nonglobal, so LOCAL alone cannot solve the problem. Nonregular Reinhardt nonagon with headings 0,20,100,120,140,220,240,260,340 degrees has FULL H triangle+leaves, admits a nonmax physical 7-edge forest stress even though that same graph has no proper stress at regular reference. Cannot transfer arbitrary target Farkas obstruction to regular. For N=2m with odd m, classical two-step-per-carrier-arc Reinhardt unit rim is only Theta(1/D) from the regular even unit rim, but not central. Thus no fixed-radius central robustness exclusion. Near-even pure matching/core exclusion radius tan(pi/(2N))/8 already proved, no uniform stress assumption.

Other checked tools: loaded endpoints within eps less1/(4D) of M packing lattices(minvector1), with z exceptions, obey ceilD at most z+M*(3[pi(D+2eps)]^(2/3)+2[...]^(1/3)+1); z0 impossible D at least326 M^3. An actual odd D cycle yields Reuleaux carrier containing all P. If convex hull is an entirely unit-edged fully-D-loaded rim and H contains a cycle, every hull vertex lies on carrier boundary and chord angle sum gives D=1/[2sin(pi/(2N))], exactly Reinhardt. This says nothing for H forest or unloaded hull vertices.

ROOT conjectural exact candidate formula: for N convex labels, covering convex-thrackle forests with c>=2 components (N-c internal edges, no isolates), F_c(N)=N/(2c)*2^(N-2c)*binom(N-c-1,c-1), 2c<=N. c2 is proved earlier, c3 matches all exact counts7,120,1232,9984,70400 atN7..15. RESULT: COMPLETE PROOF OF THE PROPOSED FORMULA FOR EVERY c >= 2

Theorem (covering convex-thrackle forest enumeration).

Let N >= 2c, c >= 2. Place N distinctly labeled points in
strictly convex position, in a prescribed cyclic order.

Let F_c(N) count spanning forests satisfying:

1. Exactly c connected components.
2. Every component has at least two vertices (no isolates).
3. Every two edges intersect, either at a common endpoint
   or by a proper crossing.

Then

F_c(N) = [N/(2c)] * 2^(N-2c) * binom(N-c-1,c-1).

Moreover, every such forest has a unique decomposition,
up to cyclic starting position, into 2c nonempty consecutive
vertex blocks

A_1, A_2, ..., A_c, B_1, B_2, ..., B_c,

where component i is a monotone grid-path tree between
A_i and B_i.

Proof.

STEP 1. A component separated by an external chord is a
monotone grid-path tree.

Fix a component T. Since c >= 2, choose an edge e belonging
to another component.

Every edge of T must properly cross e because the components
have disjoint vertex sets.

The endpoints of e divide the circle into two open arcs.
Write the vertices of T on these arcs as

U = (u_1,...,u_a),
V = (v_1,...,v_b),

both ordered clockwise.

Both sets are nonempty, and every edge of T joins U to V.

Represent the edge u_p v_q by the integer pair (p,q).

For two such edges, the convex-thrackle condition says that
their coordinate pairs are comparable in the product order.

Indeed, edges sharing an endpoint are comparable. For four
distinct endpoints with p < r, the chords u_p v_q and
u_r v_s cross precisely when q < s.

Thus all edge pairs form a chain in the product order.

List the edges in increasing order:

(p_1,q_1),...,(p_m,q_m).

Because T is a tree on a+b vertices,

m = a+b-1.

Since every vertex belongs to an edge, the first pair is
(1,1) and the last pair is (a,b).

Consecutive pairs must share a coordinate.

Otherwise, if both coordinates increase strictly between
consecutive pairs t and t+1, all edges up to t have both
coordinates at most (p_t,q_t), while all later edges have
both coordinates at least (p_(t+1),q_(t+1)).

No edge in the first group then shares a vertex with an edge
in the second group. This contradicts connectivity of T.

Consequently each consecutive pair increases exactly one
coordinate by a positive integer.

There are

m-1 = a+b-2

transitions. Their total coordinate increment is

(a-1)+(b-1) = a+b-2.

Therefore every transition increases exactly one coordinate
by exactly 1.

The edges of T consequently trace a monotone lattice path
from (1,1) to (a,b), using steps (1,0) and (0,1).

In particular, consecutive U-vertices u_p,u_(p+1) have a
common V-neighbor. Likewise consecutive V-vertices have
a common U-neighbor.

The number of possible component trees for fixed ordered
sets U,V is therefore exactly

binom(a+b-2,a-1).

STEP 2. Each bipartition class is a consecutive block in
the FULL circular label sequence.

Consider consecutive U-vertices u_p,u_(p+1).

By Step 1, they share some neighbor v_q, so both

u_p v_q and u_(p+1) v_q

are edges of T.

Suppose another label x lies strictly between u_p and
u_(p+1) clockwise.

It cannot belong to T: there are no intervening U-vertices
by definition, and all V-vertices occupy the opposite arc
of e.

Hence x belongs to another component and is incident to
some edge xz, because there are no isolates.

The clockwise order of the relevant vertices is

u_p, x, u_(p+1), v_q.

For xz to cross u_p v_q, its other endpoint z must lie in
the open clockwise arc (v_q,u_p).

For xz to cross u_(p+1) v_q, z must instead lie in the
disjoint open clockwise arc (u_(p+1),v_q).

This is impossible.

Therefore no label lies between consecutive U-vertices.

The same argument, interchanging U and V, proves that
consecutive V-vertices also have no intervening labels.

Thus U and V are each uninterrupted blocks in the full
circular label sequence.

Since T is connected, its bipartition is unique up to
interchanging its two classes. Hence these two blocks are
intrinsic to T, independently of which external edge e
was initially selected.

STEP 3. Global order of the 2c blocks.

Apply Step 2 to every component.

Each component T_i has exactly two nonempty consecutive
blocks, denoted temporarily A_i and B_i.

Choose one edge from each component.

These c edges have pairwise disjoint endpoints and cross
pairwise.

A collection of c pairwise crossing chords on 2c circular
endpoints necessarily has cyclic endpoint order

1,2,...,c,1,2,...,c,

up to relabeling and cyclic rotation.

To see this, choose one chord. Every other chord has one
endpoint in each of its complementary arcs. If two other
chords have their first endpoints in a particular order on
one arc, their second endpoints must occur in that same
clockwise order on the other arc; otherwise those two
chords would not cross.

Because each selected endpoint belongs to one of the
already established uninterrupted component blocks, the
blocks themselves have this cyclic order.

Thus, after naming the components appropriately, the
entire labeled circle is partitioned as

A_1,...,A_c,B_1,...,B_c.

Every edge of component i joins A_i to B_i.

This proves the proposed global structural decomposition.

STEP 4. Converse: every such block-path specification works.

Choose positive block sizes a_i,b_i and arrange the blocks
in the indicated cyclic order.

Inside component i, choose any monotone grid path from
(1,1) to (a_i,b_i), interpreting its lattice points as
edges.

By Step 1 in reverse, these edges form a tree spanning
A_i union B_i, and every two edges of that tree meet.

For i < j, every point in A_i precedes every point in A_j,
and every point in B_i precedes every point in B_j, with
all A-blocks preceding all B-blocks.

Thus every A_i--B_i chord properly crosses every
A_j--B_j chord.

The resulting graph is therefore a covering convex-thrackle
forest with exactly c nontrivial components.

The construction is both necessary and sufficient.

STEP 5. Exact enumeration.

First choose a starting block boundary, giving N choices
on the labeled circle.

For positive sizes satisfying

sum_i(a_i+b_i) = N,

the number of monotone-path choices is

product_i binom(a_i+b_i-2,a_i-1).

Write n_i = a_i+b_i >= 2.

For fixed n_i, summing over positive a_i,b_i gives

sum_(a_i=1)^(n_i-1) binom(n_i-2,a_i-1)
    = 2^(n_i-2).

Therefore, for fixed component sizes n_1,...,n_c, the
number of path choices summed over their block splits is

product_i 2^(n_i-2) = 2^(N-2c).

The number of ordered compositions

n_1+...+n_c=N,  n_i>=2

is

binom(N-c-1,c-1).

Hence the number of rooted block specifications is

N * 2^(N-2c) * binom(N-c-1,c-1).

Every forest occurs exactly 2c times in this count,
once for each choice of its starting block.

There are no additional identifications: the components
and their two bipartition blocks are intrinsically
determined by the forest.

Dividing by 2c proves

F_c(N) = [N/(2c)] * 2^(N-2c) * binom(N-c-1,c-1).

QED.


CHECKS AND SCOPE

For c=3 this gives, successively at N=7,9,11,13,15,

7, 120, 1232, 9984, 70400,

agreeing with the supplied exact counts.

I also independently executed direct finite enumeration
for (N,c)=(6,2),(6,3),(7,2),(7,3),(8,3).
The resulting counts were respectively

18, 1, 56, 7, 32,

all agreeing with the formula. These finite checks are
not used in the proof.

The c=1 case is excluded because Step 1 requires an edge
from a different component. No extension to c=1 is claimed.

This is a combinatorial theorem about convex thrackles.
It does not impose equal Euclidean edge lengths, physical
stress, or common diameter D. Consequently it neither
settles the regular odd-rim stress question nor establishes
the full global Erdos Problem #99.

SOURCES AND ATTRIBUTION

Ruy Fabila-Monroy, Jakob Jonsson, Pavel Valtr, and
David R. Wood, "The exact chromatic number of the convex
segment disjointness graph" (2018), Section 2.
Primary source:
https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.01057
Direct PDF:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.01057

Their paper defines convex thrackles and records the
standard maximal convex-thrackle structure (odd cycle
with pendant vertices). The proof above does not invoke
that classification.

Erdos Problem #99, original problem statement:
https://www.erdosproblems.com/99

The proposed formula and its previously checked numerical
values were supplied in the research notes. The arbitrary-c
proof here is self-contained; no historical novelty or
publication priority is asserted.

BOTTOM LINE

The conjectural exact formula is proved for every c>=2,
2c<=N, under the stated no-isolates convex-thrackle
definition. Both the full-label block structure and the
monotone-grid-path enumeration follow without additional
geometric or stress assumptions.

RESULT: AN INFINITE EXACT RANK AND PHYSICAL-STRESS THRESHOLD
FOR THE LONGEST-DIAGONAL SUBCLASS OF REGULAR ODD RIMS

Status: Complete self-contained proof.
Scope: Every odd N >= 5, including all N >= 17.
The full Erdos Problem #99 remains open.

THEOREM.

Let N = 2m+1 >= 5, and let P be the regular N-gon scaled
so that consecutive vertices have distance 1.

Write
    t = pi/N,
    q = exp(2*pi*I/N),
    p_i = q^i/(2 sin t),  i modulo N.

Let R be its N rim edges {i,i+1}, and let
    e_i = {i,i+m},  i modulo N
be its N longest diagonals, all of length

DISCRETE SYMMETRY OBSTRUCTION FOR REGULAR ODD UNIT RIMS

Status: Complete elementary finite-N proof.
Scope: Arbitrary centers and all admissible label involutions.
No global optimality or solution of Erdos Problem #99 is claimed.

THEOREM

Let N=2m+1 >= 3 be odd, and let

  p_j = R exp(2*pi*i*j/N),  j=0,...,N-1,
  R = 1/(2 sin(pi/N)).

Identify the complex plane with R^2. Write P_N={p_j}, and set

  a = 2R sin(pi/(2N))
    = 1/(2 cos(pi/(2N))).

For any finite labeled configuration X, define

  delta(X) =
    min over admissible involutions f and centers c
    max_j |x_j+x_f(j)-2c|,

where f^2=id and f has at most one fixed label.

Then:

(A) Odd rim:

  R + R/(N-1) <= delta(P_N) <= R + a/2.

(B) Rim with an additional center label:

Let Q_N=P_N union {0}, with 0 a new label. Then

  R/2 + R/(N-1) <= delta(Q_N) <= R/2 + a/2.

Both assertions permit arbitrary centers and arbitrary
admissible involutions, not merely geometric reflections.

(C) Convex-hull comparison:

Writing K_N=conv(P_N),

  d_H(K_N,-K_N) = R(1-cos(pi/N)).

In particular, if D_N is the actual diameter of P_N,

  D_N = 2R cos(pi/(2N)),

then, as odd N tends to infinity,

  delta(P_N) = D_N/2 + O(1),
  delta(Q_N) = D_N/4 + O(1),

but

  d_H(K_N,-K_N) = 1/(4D_N) + O(D_N^(-3)).

Thus arbitrarily small relative or absolute
convex-hull asymmetry does not imply small discrete
involution defect.

PROOF

1. The forced fixed label

Since N is odd, every involution of its N labels has
an odd number of fixed labels. Requiring at most one
forces exactly one.

Let f be that fixed label, and let u=p_f.

There are exactly m=(N-1)/2 two-element orbits.

For each orbit {j,k}, put s=p_j+p_k.

Since the regular rim is centered at the origin,

  sum_j p_j=0.

Consequently,

  sum_over_pairs s = -u.

The mean pair-sum vector is therefore

  s_bar = -u/m.

Put t=2c, with c completely arbitrary.

If the involution defect is at most E, then

  |2u-t| <= E

from the fixed label, and

  |s-t| <= E

for every two-element orbit.

Averaging the latter inequalities gives

  |s_bar-t| <= E.

The triangle inequality now yields

  2E >= |2u-s_bar|
      = |2u+u/m|
      = 2R+R/m.

Hence

  E >= R+R/(2m)
    = R+R/(N-1).

This proves the lower bound in (A), simultaneously
for every involution and every center.

In particular, the proposed lower bound delta>=R
is correct but not sharp as a lower estimate:
the stronger bound above holds universally.

2. Explicit involution giving the upper bound

Rotational invariance permits fixing label 0.

Pair

  j with j+m,  j=1,...,m,

and leave label 0 fixed.

This covers all N labels exactly once.

Each paired chord subtends an angle

  2*pi*m/N = pi-pi/N.

Thus every pair sum satisfies

  |p_j+p_(j+m)| = a.

Choose t=2c on the positive real axis with

  t=R-a/2.

Since a<=R for N>=3, t is nonnegative.

At the fixed vertex,

  |2p_0-t| = 2R-(R-a/2)
            = R+a/2.

For every other orbit,

  |p_j+p_(j+m)-t|
      <= |p_j+p_(j+m)|+|t|
      = a+R-a/2
      = R+a/2.

Therefore

  delta(P_N) <= R+a/2.

This completes (A).

3. Adding a center label

The configuration Q_N contains N+1 even labels.

An involution on an even number of labels has an
even number of fixed labels. Since at most one is
allowed, there are no fixed labels.

The new center label 0 must therefore pair with
some rim vertex u, where |u|=R.

The corresponding pair sum is u.

The remaining N-1 rim vertices form m pairs.
Their pair sums again have mean

  s_bar=-u/m.

For arbitrary t=2c and defect E,

  |u-t| <= E,
  |s_bar-t| <= E.

Consequently,

  2E >= |u-s_bar|
      = R+R/m.

Thus

  E >= R/2+R/(2m)
    = R/2+R/(N-1).

For the upper bound, pair the center label with
rim label 0, and use exactly the near-antipodal
rim pairing from Step 2 for the other labels.

Choose

  t=(R-a)/2

on the positive real axis.

The center/rim pair contributes

  |p_0-t| = (R+a)/2.

Every other pair contributes at most

  a+|t| = (R+a)/2.

Hence

  delta(Q_N) <= (R+a)/2.

This completes (B).

Notice that Q_N is a unit-separated configuration
for odd N>=7, since R>=1 in that range. For N=3,5
it remains a valid labeled geometric example, but
is not a unit-separated packing.

4. Convex-hull Hausdorff distance

For an odd regular N-gon, central reflection of its
convex hull is equivalent to rotation by pi/N,
modulo its rotational symmetry by 2*pi/N.

Write alpha=pi/N.

The support function of K_N in direction theta is

  h_K(theta)=R max_j cos(theta-2*pi*j/N).

The support function of -K_N is the same expression
with the vertex directions shifted by alpha.

On each interval between consecutive vertex
directions, comparison of nearest angular distances
gives

  |h_K(theta)-h_(-K)(theta)|
      <= R(1-cos(alpha)).

Equality holds in a vertex direction.

For compact convex sets, Hausdorff distance equals
the supremum of the absolute difference of their
support functions. Therefore

  d_H(K_N,-K_N)=R(1-cos(pi/N)).

Finally,

  R=N/(2*pi)+O(1/N),
  a=1/2+O(N^(-2)),
  D_N=N/pi+O(1/N).

Substitution gives all asymptotic statements in (C).

QED.


WHY THE NEAREST-REFLECTION BIJECTION IS INSUFFICIENT

Consider the cyclic permutation

  g(j)=j+m (mod N).

Every vertex has an approximately antipodal image:

  |p_j+p_g(j)|=a
             =1/(2cos(pi/(2N)))
             -> 1/2.

However,

  g^2(j)=j+2m=j-1 (mod N),

which differs from j for every N>=3.

Therefore g is not an involution.

Indeed, gcd(m,N)=1, so g is a single N-cycle.

Its small pointwise antipodal error cannot be used
as the defect of a centrally symmetric labeling.

The exact obstruction is not simply that the
nearest reflected label is displaced by about 1/2.

It is that reciprocal pairing imposes an orbit
structure incompatible with the nearest-reflection
permutation. For odd N, one fixed label is forced.
Its pair-sum vector is 2u, while the mean pair-sum
vector of the remaining labels is -u/m.

Those two vectors are separated by approximately 2R.
No choice of center can eliminate this separation.

Adding a center label removes the forced fixed
orbit, but its pairing with a rim vertex still
creates a pair-sum vector of length R. Thus even
the augmented configuration has defect of order R.

CONSEQUENCE FOR CENTRAL ROBUSTNESS ARGUMENTS

There are three quantitatively different notions:

  Hull Hausdorff defect:       Theta(1/D)
  Nearest reflected labels:   Theta(1)
  Admissible involution:      Theta(D)

The first two do not control the third.

In particular, a theorem requiring a small
all-label involution defect cannot be applied to
large regular odd rims solely because their hulls
are nearly centrally symmetric.

The additional center label reduces the leading
involution defect by a factor of two, but does not
make it bounded independently of N.

This gives a rigorous obstruction to replacing
discrete central symmetry by approximate symmetry
of the convex hull.

It does not contradict the centrally symmetric
local-minimum classification in the supplied notes.
The odd rims are not centrally symmetric as labeled
point configurations, and their discrete symmetry
defect grows with diameter.

Moreover,

In a strictly convex polygon, each directed edge direction
occurs at most once along the positively oriented boundary.
Thus each unoriented direction occurs at most twice.

The two endpoint sides of a good-good track therefore have
opposite directed orientations.

Now consider good-good tracks of different directions.

Their four endpoint sides alternate around the convex hull:
the corresponding outward normal directions occur in
antipodal pairs, and two distinct antipodal pairs interlace
on the circle.

Two curves inside a convex disk joining alternating
boundary endpoints must intersect.

Hence these two tracks cross in a common rhombus.

At that crossing, their edge directions are the two side
directions of the rhombus. Their acute angular separation
is strictly greater than 60 degrees.

There cannot be three unoriented line directions whose
pairwise acute separations are all strictly greater than
60 degrees: arranging three directions modulo 180 degrees
gives three cyclic gaps summing to 180 degrees, so one gap
is at most 60 degrees.

Consequently there are at most two good-good tracks,
one for each possible direction.

They account for at most four good outer traversals.    (2)

Notice that no claim was made that arbitrary tracks in a
nonconvex quadrilateral patch must cross. Convex-hull
endpoints on BOTH tracks are essential.

E. Charging all remaining good traversals

Let P_bad be the sum of the perimeters of all bounded
nonquadrilateral faces.

Every such face has length l >= 5, and

   l <= 5(l-4).

Therefore

   P_bad <= 5delta.                         (3)

Consider a good outer traversal not belonging to a
good-good track.

There are three exhaustive possibilities.

(i) It is incident to a nonquadrilateral bounded face.

Charge it to that face-side incidence.

(ii) It is incident to a quadrilateral face.

Start its track. Since the track is not good-good, its
opposite end lies either at a bad outer traversal or
at a side of a nonquadrilateral face.

Charge the starting traversal to that endpoint.

(iii) Its physical edge is a bridge.

A bridge borders no bounded face and appears twice on
the outer facial walk.

Charge the good traversal to its reverse traversal,
which must be bad.

Indeed, if both orientations were good, the unique chosen
occurrence at each endpoint would use the bridge both
incoming and outgoing. Both endpoints would then have
degree one, forcing connected C to be a single edge,
contrary to noncollinearity.

All these charges are injective.

For (i), the charged outer face-side incidence is unique.
For (ii), each nonquadrilateral face-side or bad outer
edge is the endpoint of at most one rhombus track.
For (iii), reverse traversals belong to distinct bridges.

Moreover, an edge charged under (i) cannot simultaneously
be a quad-facing track endpoint under (ii), and a bridge
cannot be adjacent to a quadrilateral face.

Thus no capacity is counted twice.

There are at most 2q bad outer traversals, by the
boundary-occurrence count in part A.

Combining (2) and (3) gives

   M <= 4+P_bad+2q
     <= 4+5delta+2q.                        (4)

F. Final inequality

Equations (1) and (4) imply

   h-q <= 4+5delta+2q,

hence

   h <= 4+5delta+3q
     <= 4+5(delta+q).

The supplied outer-face inequality yields

   delta+q
     = b-h+delta
     <= 2k-h
     = eta.

Therefore

   h <= 4+5eta.

This proves the theorem.

QED.

Because every loaded vertex has diameter degree at least one,

   eta = sum_over_loaded_vertices (deg_H(v)-1).

The theorem forces this total degree excess to be linear in
the number of loaded diameter endpoints.

It does NOT force a positive fraction of loaded vertices to
have degree greater than one: all excess could, in principle,
be concentrated at comparatively few vertices.

It also does not exclude triangle-free global minimizers.
The bound is conditional on the selected-core normal form,
particularly strict exposure of all loaded endpoints and
b+delta <= 2k.

No passage from an original joint-MAX stress support to a
selected representative is used or established here.

with joint-MAX positive physical stress and PSD stress matrix, but
with an explicit diameter-decreasing pinwheel motion.

This is a rigorous restricted no-go for a natural four-arm mesh
construction. It is NOT an ordinary local minimum and does NOT

PROPOSITION

For every integer L >= 1 there is a unit-separated planar packing
P_L with

    n = 4(L+1),
    D = 2L + sqrt(2),

satisfying all the following:

1. Its FULL unit graph F is triangle-free and consists of a unit
   square with four outward straight unit-contact arms, each of
   length L.

2. Its FULL diameter graph H consists of exactly two edges, joining
   opposite arm tips.

3. A physical stress is strictly positive on EVERY edge of F and
   EVERY edge of H. Consequently it is joint MAX.

4. Omega = L_F(mu) - L_H(lambda) is PSD, with kernel exactly
   span(1,x,y).

5. Nevertheless P_L is not an ordinary local diameter minimum:
   an explicit arbitrarily small feasible motion strictly decreases
   its actual diameter.

In particular, L=4 gives n=20 and D=8+sqrt(2)>9, with a bounded
unit-square face carrying four strictly positive contact multipliers.

CONSTRUCTION

Index the four corners by (s,t), where s,t belong to {-1,+1}.

Put

    q_(s,t) = (s/2,t/2),
    u_(s,t) = (s,t)/sqrt(2).

RESULT: ALL-ODD REGULAR-RIM STRESS-SUPPORT THEOREM

Status: Complete analytic proof, for every odd N >= 5.
No enumeration, positivity assumption, or forest classification needed.
The full Erdős Problem #99 remains unsolved.

THEOREM

Let N = 2m+1 >= 5 be odd, and let P be the regular N-gon
scaled so that its consecutive sides have length 1.

Its full unit-contact graph F is the boundary N-cycle. Its full
diameter graph H consists of the N edges

    {j,j+m},   j in Z/NZ.

Suppose real, not necessarily nonnegative, edge weights mu on F
and lambda on H satisfy

    L_F(mu) P = L_H(lambda) P.

Then either all weights vanish, or there exist real a,b,c, not
all zero, such that

    lambda_j = a + b cos(2*pi*j/N) + c sin(2*pi*j/N)

for every j.

Consequently every nonzero equilibrium stress has at least N-2
nonzero diameter-edge weights.

In particular, no subset of at most N-3 diameter edges supports
a nonzero equilibrium stress, even if all N contact edges are
available and signed weights are allowed.

This excludes, uniformly in N, every covering convex-thrackle
forest with at least three components. It also excludes arbitrary
diameter-edge subsets of cardinality at most N-3.

PROOF

1. Complex coordinates and equilibrium equations.

Let

    w = exp(2*pi*i/N),    alpha = pi/N,

and use vertex coordinates

    z_j = w^j.

Scaling all coordinates by the same positive constant does not
change the equilibrium equations, so the normalization of the
side length is immaterial.

Write mu_j for the weight on {j,j+1}, and lambda_j for the
weight on {j,j+m}. Indices are interpreted modulo N.

At vertex j the two incident contact edges are indexed j and
j-1; the two incident diameter edges are indexed j and j-m.

The vector equilibrium equation, expressed as a complex equation
and divided by z_j, is

 (1-w)mu_j + (1-w^(-1))mu_(j-1)
   = (1-w^m)lambda_j + (1-w^(-m))lambda_(j-m).       (1)

This equation is exact, with no positivity requirement.

2. Fourier diagonalization.

For any real N-periodic sequence u define

    uhat_q = sum_(j=0)^(N-1) u_j w^(-q*j).

Taking the discrete Fourier transform of (1) gives

    A_q muhat_q = B_q lambdahat_q,                  (2)

where

    A_q = (1-w)(1-w^(-(q+1))),

    B_q = (1-w^m)(1-w^(-m*(q+1))).

For q = 2,...,m, both A_q and A_(-q) are nonzero.
Set

    R_q = B_q/A_q.

Then

    muhat_q = R_q lambdahat_q,
    muhat_(-q) = R_(-q) lambdahat_(-q).

Since the original weights are real,

    muhat_(-q) = conjugate(muhat_q),
    lambdahat_(-q) = conjugate(lambdahat_q).

Therefore a nonzero lambdahat_q requires

    R_(-q) = conjugate(R_q).                         (3)

We prove that (3) is impossible for 2 <= q <= m.

3. Exact trigonometric obstruction.

Define

    K = sin(m*alpha)/sin(alpha) > 0,

    f(t) = sin(m*t*alpha)/sin(t*alpha).

Using

    1-exp(2*i*x) = -2*i*exp(i*x)*sin(x),

we obtain

    R_q = K exp(-i*(m-1)*q*alpha) f(q+1),

    R_(-q) = K exp(i*(m-1)*q*alpha) f(q-1).

Here f(-t)=f(t) was used in the second formula.

Consequently (3) is equivalent to

    f(q-1) = f(q+1).                                 (4)

But N=2m+1 implies

    m*alpha = pi/2 - alpha/2.

Thus, for positive integer t<N,

    f(t) = (-1)^s / (2*sin(t*alpha/2))
           if t=2s+1,

    f(t) = (-1)^(s+1) / (2*cos(t*alpha/2))
           if t=2s.

All denominators are strictly positive for 1 <= t < N.

It follows immediately that

    f(t)*f(t+2) < 0

whenever 1 <= t and t+2 < N.

For 2 <= q <= m we have

    1 <= q-1 < q+1 <= m+1 < N.

Hence

    f(q-1)*f(q+1) < 0.

Equation (4) is impossible.

Therefore

    lambdahat_q = 0,     q=2,...,m.

By conjugate symmetry the negative-frequency coefficients
also vanish:

    lambdahat_(-q) = 0,  q=2,...,m.

4. Exact form of the diameter weights.

Since N=2m+1, the residue classes

    0, +1, -1, +2, -2, ..., +m, -m

exhaust Z/NZ.

The only possibly nonzero Fourier coefficients of lambda
are therefore those at frequencies 0,+1,-1.

Fourier inversion yields

    lambda_j = a + b cos(2*pi*j/N)
                 + c sin(2*pi*j/N)

for real a,b,c.

If lambda is identically zero, equation (1) shows that mu
also vanishes: at every vertex the two incident contact
edge vectors are linearly independent, so both contact
weights must be zero.

Thus a nonzero stress has (a,b,c) not all zero.

5. The support bound.

Consider

    a + b cos(theta) + c sin(theta) = 0.

If b=c=0, this equation has no solution unless a=0.
Otherwise it describes the intersection of the unit circle

    x^2+y^2=1

with the straight line

    a+b*x+c*y=0.

A straight line intersects a circle in at most two points.

Therefore a nonzero trigonometric polynomial of this form
vanishes at at most two distinct vertex angles

    theta_j = 2*pi*j/N.

At least N-2 diameter weights are nonzero.

This proves the theorem.


COROLLARY: ALL COVERING FORESTS WITH >=3 COMPONENTS

Let G be any spanning forest contained in the regular odd
rim's full diameter graph H, and suppose G has c>=3
connected components.

Every forest on N vertices with c components has

    |E(G)| = N-c <= N-3.

If an equilibrium stress had diameter support contained in
G, extending its weights by zero to all of H would give a
stress with at most N-3 nonzero diameter weights.

The theorem forces this stress to vanish.

Thus no such forest supports any nonzero signed equilibrium
stress, and in particular none supports a physical
nonnegative equilibrium stress.

The conjectured component word

    A1 A2 ... Ac A1 A2 ... Ac

and its monotone internal paths are irrelevant: the
obstruction holds for every arrangement of the omitted
diameter edges.

This proves an all-odd version of the finite N<=15
regular-rim rank exclusions described in the supplied notes.


SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS

The theorem relies essentially on the regular geometry and
the two cyclic edge orbits of the equilibrium equations.

It does not establish the analogous result for irregular
Reinhardt rims. In particular, it does not contradict the
supplied irregular N=9 wall configuration with a proper
six-diameter-edge stress.

It also does not automatically apply when additional
vertices contribute unit-contact forces at the rim vertices.
Such forces modify equation (1).

Nor does the result exclude ordinary local minima: a regular
odd rim can carry equilibrium stresses using all N diameter
edges. Indeed, constant positive lambda_j and constant
positive mu_j provide an equilibrium stress.

The conclusion is therefore an exact obstruction to sparse
diameter-stress support, not an exclusion of regular odd
local minima or a same-n global competitor construction.

The unsolved global problem still requires controlling
nonregular configurations, interior populations, and
possible zero-weight attachments.

The Fourier-support argument and the all-N conclusion above

3. Archit Das (2026),

   minimum-diameter problem (Problem #99)".

(3) C is triangle-free.
(4) Every vertex in a distinguished set S is strictly exposed in
    conv(V(C)).
(5) The outer-face walk has length b, counted with multiplicity.
(6) delta = sum_f (length(f)-4), over bounded faces.

Write h=|S| and q=b-h.

Then

Consequently, if the selected physical-core inequality

             b + delta <= 2k

             h <= 4 + 5 eta.                       (2)

The theorem uses no stress, PSD, local-minimality, or diameter
hypothesis beyond those needed to establish its stated premises.

PROOF

1. Canonical outer visits.

Let K=conv(V(C)). Initially suppose K has dimension two.

At each strictly exposed vertex s, all incident graph edges lie
inside its convex-hull tangent cone. The complementary exterior
angular sector is contained in exactly one outer-face corner.
Choose that occurrence of s on the outer walk.

These are the canonical visits.

They occur in convex-hull cyclic order, even when the outer walk
repeats edges and vertices.

To verify this assertion rigorously, take a sufficiently small
closed regular neighborhood N of the embedded connected graph.
Its exterior boundary is one Jordan curve, obtained by rounding
the outer walk at vertices and following the two sides of bridges.

Choose O in int(K). From every hull vertex z, extend the ray
O+t(z-O), t>=1, outward toward a sufficiently large enclosing
circle. Distinct such rays are disjoint outside K and occur on
the enclosing circle in hull cyclic order.

Their initial portions meet the exterior boundary of N at the
corners representing the canonical visits. Disjoint arcs in the
exterior of a Jordan curve preserve their cyclic boundary order.
Thus the canonical visits occur in hull order.

In particular:

CLAIM A. If an outer-edge traversal has canonical visits at both
ends, its geometric edge is a convex-hull side.

Indeed, otherwise the chord between its distinct hull vertices
would have at least one hull vertex strictly between its endpoints
on each of the two hull arcs. The canonical visit of a hull vertex
on the arc corresponding to that traversal would have to occur
between its endpoints on the outer walk, which is impossible.

This argument uses canonical visits, not arbitrary occurrences
of exposed vertices. That distinction is essential at cutvertices.

2. Good and bad traversals.

Call an outer-edge traversal good if both endpoint visits are
chosen canonical visits of S. Otherwise call it bad.

There are exactly q unchosen visits. Each visit is incident to
two outer-walk traversals, so, writing t for the number of bad
traversals,

                    t <= 2q.                       (3)

Every good traversal is a unit convex-hull side, by Claim A.

Since its endpoints are strictly exposed, it is not part of a
longer subdivided straight hull side. In particular, for each
oriented hull-side direction there is at most one good edge.

3. Rhombus tracks terminate.

Every bounded quadrilateral face is a convex unit rhombus.

Its acute angle is strictly greater than 60 degrees: otherwise
its shorter diagonal has length at most one. Strict inequality
follows because equality would create a unit equilateral
triangle in the full unit-contact graph.

Construct a track by entering a rhombus through an edge and
exiting through the opposite, parallel edge. Continue across
that edge whenever its other incident face is another rhombus.

All edges crossed by a track have one fixed unoriented direction
v.

A track cannot form a cycle. To see this, choose a normal n to v
and orient the track so that its first rhombus lies on the
positive-n side of its entering edge.

Opposite sides of a nondegenerate rhombus have strictly ordered
n-coordinates. Across the exiting edge, the next rhombus lies
on the opposite side from the previous rhombus, hence again
on the positive-n side in the direction of travel.

Thus the n-coordinate of successive crossed edges strictly
increases. Finiteness implies termination.

Each track therefore has two distinct terminal edges. Its
terminal sides are incident, on the other side, to either the
outer face or a bounded nonquadrilateral face.

No simply-connectedness assumption on the union of rhombi is
used.

4. Tracks with two good outer endpoints.

Suppose a track terminates at two good outer edges.

Both are convex-hull sides by Claim A, and both are parallel
to v. Since their endpoints are strictly exposed, they must
occupy opposite support sides of K.

Consider two such tracks with distinct unoriented directions
v and w.

Their terminal sides alternate in cyclic order around K:
the outward normals are n_v, n_w, -n_v, -n_w, in one of the
two possible alternating orders.

Their track arcs, drawn through edge midpoints and rhombus
interiors, must therefore intersect by the Jordan crosscut
argument.

An intersection can occur only inside a rhombus crossed by
both tracks. Hence the acute angle between v and w is
strictly greater than 60 degrees.

It follows that there are at most two distinct directions
of good-good tracks. Indeed, three unoriented directions
on a circle of circumference 180 degrees necessarily have
some pair at angular distance at most 60 degrees.

For each direction, there are at most two good hull edges
parallel to it, and each belongs to only one track.

Therefore:

CLAIM B. All good-good tracks together account for at most
four good outer-edge traversals.

This crossing argument applies only to good-good tracks.
It makes no assertion that arbitrary tracks of a nonconvex
rhombus complex intersect.

5. Charging all remaining good traversals.

There are three possibilities.

(A) A good outer traversal is adjacent to a bounded
nonquadrilateral face.

Charge it to that face-edge incidence.

For a face of length l>=5,

                    l <= 5(l-4).

Consequently all bounded nonquadrilateral faces collectively
supply at most 5 delta such incidences.

(B) A good outer traversal is adjacent to a rhombus.

Follow its unique track. Unless its other endpoint is good,
already counted by Claim B, that endpoint is either:

  - a bad outer traversal; or
  - an edge incident to a bounded nonquadrilateral face.

Charge the starting good traversal to that endpoint.

This assignment is injective within each endpoint class:
a rhombus edge has exactly one track direction, so a terminal
edge cannot receive charges from two different tracks.
Likewise a nonquadrilateral face-edge incidence has at most
one rhombus on its opposite side.

(C) A good outer traversal belongs to a bridge.

A bridge has two outer-walk traversals and no incident bounded
face. Its opposite traversal is bad unless both bridge
endpoints have graph degree one.

For a connected graph with at least three vertices, the latter
case is impossible: at a vertex of degree at least two, the two
sides of a bridge belong to different outer-face corners.

Charge the good bridge traversal to its opposite bad traversal.

These bridge charges cannot collide with charges from (B),
because a bridge is not incident to a rhombus.

Nor can charges in (A) collide with terminal-incidence charges
in (B): an edge charged directly in (A) has the outer face on
its opposite side, whereas a terminal incidence charged in
(B) has a rhombus there.

Thus the complete charge is jointly injective, except for the
four explicitly allowed good-good endpoints.

Writing g for the number of good outer traversals gives

                    g <= 4 + 5 delta + t.           (4)

Since b=g+t, equations (3) and (4) yield

                    b <= 4 + 5 delta + 2t
                      <= 4 + 5 delta + 4q.

Substituting b=h+q proves

                    h <= 4 + 5 delta + 3q.

Finally,

                    q + delta <= 2k-h = eta,

so

                    5 delta + 3q <= 5 eta.

This proves (2).

If K is one-dimensional, it has at most two strictly exposed
vertices, so h<=2 and the conclusion is immediate.

QED.

Then

In particular,

The positive equilibrium stress gives a nontrivial
linear dependence among the e+k mixed rigidity rows.
Since their rank is 2r-3,

    s := e+k-(2r-2) >= 0.

Let b be the outer-face boundary-walk length, counted
with multiplicity. Define

    Q = sum_f (length(f)-4),

over bounded faces.

All bounded faces have length at least four, so Q>=0.

Euler's formula and face incidence give

Consequently,

All h diameter endpoints occur on the outer walk.

Put

Let f count bounded faces of length at least five,

Next construct rhombic trains.

For each quadrilateral face, join the midpoints of
its opposite edges. Continuing through adjacent
quadrilaterals produces tracks with constant
unoriented edge direction.

These tracks cannot close into cycles. Indeed, fix
the direction u of their transverse contact edges.
Orient the normal to u toward the next rhombus.
Each track step has strictly positive projection on
this normal. This orientation remains consistent
when crossing a shared contact edge.

Hence all tracks are finite paths.

Let N4 denote the number of quadrilateral faces,
and let t denote the number of tracks, including
singleton-edge tracks.

Each quadrilateral contributes exactly two links
between contact-edge states. Since the track graph
is a forest,

    t = e-2N4.

Face incidence gives

    2e = b+4N4+5f+g.

Therefore

We now bound the number of tracks having both ends

Choose one outer-walk occurrence of each exposed
diameter endpoint, in cyclic order. Divide the outer
walk into h intervals joining consecutive endpoints.

An interval is good if it consists of one contact
edge. Every good interval is a unit convex-hull side.

There are b-h=x excess edge occurrences beyond the
mandatory one per interval.

Thus at most x intervals are bad, and their total
number of edge occurrences is at most 2x.

Every train endpoint not on the outer face lies
along an edge incident to a nonquadrilateral face.
The total capacity of these exceptional incidences

Call a train good if both endpoints belong to good
convex-hull sides.

There are at most two good trains.

To prove this, observe first that a good train joins
two parallel hull sides with opposite orientations.
For a convex polygon, any fixed unoriented direction
can occur in at most two genuine hull sides, with
opposite orientations. Distinct good trains therefore
have distinct projective directions.

For any two distinct good trains, their four endpoints
alternate around the convex boundary. Their embedded
track arcs must consequently intersect.

Such an intersection occurs inside a shared rhombus.
Unit separation and triangle-freeness force the acute
angle between its two side directions to exceed
60 degrees: otherwise its shorter diagonal has
length at most one.

Hence every pair of good train directions has
projective angular separation strictly above
60 degrees.

Three such directions are impossible on a projective
circle of circumference 180 degrees.

Therefore at most two trains are good.

Every remaining train consumes at least one bad
endpoint incidence. Thus

Substitute (5):

or

This proves the first assertion.

Since h=2k-R and k<=3R+2,

Let P be a unit-separated planar configuration of actual diameter
D >= 9. Assume its triangle-free unit-contact core C satisfies:

(A1) C is connected and contains every actual diameter endpoint.

(A2) Its mixed contact/diameter rigidity matrix has rank 2r-3,

(A3) A nonzero physical equilibrium stress exists on these rows.

(A4) Every bounded face has length at least four.

Then the FULL actual diameter graph H cannot be a star.

number of actual diameter edges, b for the outer-face walk length

    delta = sum_faces (face_length - 4) >= 0.

STEP 1. Verify the face-count inequality independently.

Since C is a connected plane graph, Euler's formula gives

    f = m-r+1,

where f counts bounded faces.

Every edge contributes twice to the total face-boundary length,
including the outer face. Consequently,

    4f+delta = 2m-b.

Substitution yields

    b+delta = 4r-2m-4.                         (1)

The mixed rigidity matrix has m+k rows and rank 2r-3.
The physical equilibrium stress supplies a nonzero linear
dependence among these rows. Therefore

    m+k >= 2r-2.

Using (1),

    b+delta <= 2k.                            (2)

Thus (2) follows from Euler, rank, and stress dependence. It
does not require the unverified linear branch inequality.

STEP 2. Diameter partners occupy a 60-degree arc.

Suppose H is a star centered at the PACKING POINT p0.

Let its k partners be q1,...,qk. Translate p0 to the origin.
Every partner lies on the circle of radius D:

    |qj| = D.

Because D is the diameter of the entire packing,

    |qi-qj| <= D

For two radius-D vectors with smaller angular separation theta,

    |qi-qj| = 2D sin(theta/2).

Therefore theta <= pi/3.

It remains to verify that pairwise angular separation at most
pi/3 implies containment in ONE arc of length pi/3.

Fix q1 at angle zero. Every other angle can be represented
in [-pi/3,pi/3].

If angles occur on both sides, let a >= 0 and -c <= 0 be the
largest positive and smallest negative angles. Their ordinary
separation is a+c <= 2pi/3 < pi.

The diameter constraint on these two partners forces

    2D sin((a+c)/2) <= D,

hence a+c <= pi/3.

If all angles have one sign, the containment is immediate.

Thus all partners lie in a closed arc of angular length <= pi/3.
This establishes the claimed 60-degree confinement without
assuming central symmetry.

STEP 3. Angular unit separation.

Order the partners along this arc.

For consecutive partners, write their angular difference as
theta_j. Unit separation implies

    1 <= 2D sin(theta_j/2) <= D theta_j.

Therefore

    theta_j >= 1/D.

Summing the k-1 consecutive differences gives

    (k-1)/D <= pi/3,

so

The sharper inequality is

No assumption about the other packing points is needed.

STEP 4. Verify the exact hull perimeter estimate.

Consider

    K = conv{p0,q1,...,qk}.

Every qj is an exposed vertex of K: the tangent to the
radius-D circle at qj strictly separates qj from all other
points in this subset.

The partners lie within an angular sector of width <= pi/3.
Thus p0 is also an exposed vertex.

The boundary of K consists of the two radius-D segments
joining p0 to the extreme partners, together with the
successive chords between partners.

Consequently,

    Per(K)
      = 2D + sum(j=1,...,k-1) |q(j+1)-qj|
      >= 2D+k-1.                              (4)

This is exact as a polygonal perimeter identity; the
inequality uses unit separation.

Importantly, additional core vertices need not lie in K.

Because K is contained in conv(C), convex-perimeter
monotonicity gives

    Per(conv(C)) >= Per(K).

The outer boundary walk of C has total Euclidean length b,
because every contact edge has length one. Its convex hull
equals conv(C), and the length of any closed polygonal walk
is at least the perimeter of its convex hull.

Hence

    b >= Per(conv(C)) >= 2D+k-1.              (5)

This also covers nonconvex cores, bridges, internal faces,
and arbitrarily many additional core vertices.

STEP 5. Contradiction.

Combine (2), (5), and delta >= 0:

    2D+k-1 <= b <= 2k-delta <= 2k.

Therefore

But (3) gives

This contradicts D >= 9.

THEOREM (Flat-base obstruction for an adjacent double-star).

Let P be a unit-separated planar packing of diameter D > 1.
Assume that its selected positive contact core C satisfies:

(1) Every actual diameter endpoint belongs to C.
(2) Every convex-hull corner of C is a diameter endpoint.
(3) Every active unit contact within C has positive physical
    multiplier, and every contact-core vertex has positive degree.
(4) The mixed contact/diameter bar matrix on C has rank 2r-3.

(a) All diameter endpoints lie in one closed half-plane bounded
    by AB, with A and B the only endpoints on AB.

(b) AB is a side of conv(C), but no vertex of C lies in its
    relative interior.

(c) No positive-contact edge lies along AB. Consequently, the
    positive-contact cell complex cannot fill conv(C).

    alpha=2 arcsin(1/(2D)),

that the unit-rhombus faces fill the convex hull has introduced an
additional hypothesis not supplied by the selected normal form.

Normalize A=(0,0), B=(D,0).

Write U for the leaves adjacent to A and V for the leaves
adjacent to B. Both sets are nonempty.

Step 1. Circle arcs.

For u in U, |u-A|=D and |u-B|<=D. Writing

    u=D(cos(theta),sin(theta))

gives cos(theta)>=1/2. Thus theta lies between -pi/3
and pi/3.

Similarly, each v in V lies on the radius-D circle about B,
on the arc facing A.

No leaf can lie on AB: the only point of the A-circle on
the segment AB is B itself, and similarly for the B-circle.

Step 2. Same-side confinement.

Choose u in U and v in V.

The diameter edges Au and Bv have no common endpoint.
By the diameter-edge intersection property, these segments
must cross.

If u and v lay on opposite sides of AB, their segments would
lie in opposite open half-planes and could not cross.

Fixing v and varying u shows that all U leaves lie on the
same side as v. Fixing u and varying v gives the identical
conclusion for V.

After reflection, every leaf has positive y-coordinate.

By assumption (2), every hull corner of C is among these
endpoints or A,B. Therefore

    conv(C) subset {y>=0}.

Since A and B belong to C, the segment AB is an exposed
side of conv(C).

This proves (a).

Step 3. No unloaded vertex can subdivide AB.

Suppose that an interior point z of AB is a vertex of C.

It is not a diameter endpoint, so its diameter multiplier
row vanishes.

Physical equilibrium at z reads

    sum_{zw in F(C)} mu_zw (z-w) = 0,

where every listed mu_zw is strictly positive by (3).

Take y-components. Since z_y=0 and w_y>=0,

    sum_{zw in F(C)} mu_zw w_y = 0.

Every summand is nonnegative. Hence every contact neighbor
w of z also lies on AB.

Thus all unit-contact edges incident to z are horizontal.
There is no diameter edge incident to z.

Assign velocity (0,1) to z and velocity zero to every
other core vertex. Every active mixed bar row annihilates
this velocity: contact rows at z are horizontal, and all
remaining rows have zero velocity at both endpoints.

This is a nonrigid infinitesimal motion. Indeed, it fixes
A, B and an off-axis leaf, so it cannot be a nonzero

That contradicts mixed rank 2r-3.

Therefore no such z exists, proving (b).

A positive unit-contact edge lying on AB would have to
connect two vertices of C on that segment.

By (b), the only possibilities are A and B, whose distance
is D>1.

Therefore AB contains no positive unit-contact edge.

If the bounded contact faces filled conv(C), the boundary
of that union would include AB. A finite union of closed
polygonal faces has boundary contained in its constituent
edges. Those edges are unit contacts, contradicting the
preceding paragraph.

This proves (c).

Distinct leaves in U have angular separation at least

    alpha=2 arcsin(1/(2D)),

because their mutual distance is at least one.

Their available arc has angular width at most pi/3.
Consequently,

    |U| <= 1 + pi/(3alpha).

The same argument applies to V.

polygon mixed-span rank problem.

THEOREM (boundary-cycle/chord rigidity factorization).

Let N >= 5, and let P_1,...,P_N be the successive vertices of a
regular N-gon. Let B be its boundary cycle, and let E be any set
of additional chords.

Define a real matrix W with rows indexed by

    E union {(1,N)}

and columns indexed by j=2,...,N-1.

For each row (u,v), with u<v, put

    W[(u,v),j] =
        sin(pi*(j-u)/N)*sin(pi*(v-j)/N),  if u<j<v;
        0,                              otherwise.

Let R(B union E) be the ordinary planar bar-rigidity matrix,
with one scalar row per edge.

Then

    rank R(B union E) = N-1 + rank W.                 (1)

Consequently, if E is a spanning forest with c components,
including isolated vertices, then:

(a) If c>3, the mixed rigidity matrix cannot have rank 2N-3.

(b) If c=3, the following are exactly equivalent:

    rank R(B union E) = 2N-3;
    rank W = N-2;
    det W != 0.

(c) For c=3, an entirely combinatorial necessary condition
for full rank is that the interval-incidence bipartite graph

    rows (u,v) -- columns j whenever u<j<v

has a perfect matching.

In particular, if two distinct interior indices j,k are
strictly between the endpoints of no chord in E, then W is
singular, independently of the regular polygon's geometry.

The factorization and equivalence (1) hold for every N>=5,
not just odd N. They do not require E to be a thrackle.

PROOF.

1. Exact reduction from the circle to the parabola.

Choose the angular origin so that

    phi_i = -pi/2 + pi/(2N) + pi*(i-1)/N,

and set t_i=tan(phi_i).

Thus

    t_1 < t_2 < ... < t_N,

and the circle vertices can be written

    P_i = ((1-t_i^2)/(1+t_i^2),
           2*t_i/(1+t_i^2)).

For any edge ij,

    P_i-P_j =
      2*(t_i-t_j)/((1+t_i^2)*(1+t_j^2))
      * (-(t_i+t_j), 1-t_i*t_j).

Write the original infinitesimal velocity at vertex i as
(a_i,b_i), and make the invertible vertexwise substitution

    x_i = (1+t_i^2)*b_i,
    y_i = -a_i-t_i*b_i.

Its determinant is 1+t_i^2, which is strictly positive.

The bar equation

    (P_i-P_j) dot (v_i-v_j) = 0

is therefore equivalent to

    (x_i-x_j)+(t_i+t_j)*(y_i-y_j)=0.        (2)

This proves the requisite rigidity-rank correspondence
directly, without assuming projective invariance as an
unproved auxiliary theorem.

Introduce

    z_i = x_i+2*t_i*y_i.

Equation (2) becomes

    z_i-z_j = (t_i-t_j)*(y_i+y_j).         (3)

The N-1 boundary equations on

For (c), a nonzero determinant term requires a

1. EXACT LOCAL DIFFERENCE-BODY THEOREM

Let C be the selected connected unit-contact core, with r vertices

belong to C.

Write:

  k     = number of actual diameter edges;
  h     = number of their distinct endpoints;

  delta = sum(deg(face)-4) over bounded faces;
  s     = m+k-(2r-2) >= 0;
  z     = delta+2s;
  a     = arcsin(1/(2D));

Claim:

  z <= k+1-2D*cos((k-1)*a).                 (1)

Proof.

First establish angular separation of actual diameter edges.

Every diameter endpoint is a strictly exposed vertex of the convex
hull: if |A-B|=D, projection in direction B-A is uniquely maximized
at B among all points of the packing.

Consequently, two vertex-disjoint diameter segments cross properly.
Indeed, otherwise their four exposed endpoints form a convex
quadrilateral with the two diameter segments as opposite sides.
Its crossing diagonals, meeting at X, would satisfy

  2D = |AB|+|CD|
     < |AX|+|XB|+|CX|+|XD|
     = |AC|+|BD| <= 2D,

a contradiction (with the vertices labeled in boundary order).

For diameter edges sharing an endpoint, the angle theta satisfies

  1 <= 2D*sin(theta/2) <= D,

so

  2a <= theta <= pi/3.

For disjoint diameter edges, let phi be their acute crossing angle.
Put one segment on [(0,0),(D,0)] and the other between
(x,-u) and (y,v), where u,v>0 and 0<=x<=y<=D.

If D*sin(phi)<1, then

  t=x+(D-y)=D*(1-cos(phi))<1/2.

Unit separation from the two nearby horizontal endpoints gives

  u^2+x^2 >= 1,
  v^2+(D-y)^2 >= 1.

Therefore u,v>sqrt(3)/2, contradicting

  u+v=D*sin(phi)<1.

Thus phi>=arcsin(1/D)>2a.

Every pair of projective diameter directions is therefore separated
by at least 2a.

Order the k directions around the projective circle and denote
their gaps by g_1,...,g_k. Then

  sum(g_i)=pi,  g_i>=2a.

Define the centrally symmetric direction polygon

  P_H = D*conv{+u_e,-u_e : e is a diameter edge},

where each u_e is a unit vector in its diameter direction.

Because every diameter endpoint belongs to C,

  P_H subset K-K.

For convex planar sets, perimeter is monotone under inclusion and
Minkowski-additive. Hence

  2*per(K)=per(K-K)

Concavity of sin(g/2), subject to the gap constraints, minimizes
the sum when k-1 gaps equal 2a. Therefore

  sum sin(g_i/2)

The outer contact walk is a closed unit-edge walk containing all
extreme vertices of C. Convexification cannot increase its perimeter,
including when bridges are traversed twice. Thus

Using the definition of s,

Combining this equality with (2) proves

This proves (1).

was used. The rank/stress assumptions enter only through s>=0.

over those faces. Then

Each unit rhombus connects opposite contact edges into trains.
A train has fixed projective direction. Its midpoint path can be
oriented to progress within 30 degrees of the normal to that
direction, so it cannot close. Two trains cross at most once:
when they cross, their normal directions differ by more than

cannot cross pairwise, since three projective directions cannot

SQUARE = np.array([[0., 0.], [1., 0.], [1., 1.], [0., 1.]])

def make_points(z, n):
    return np.vstack((SQUARE, z[:-1].reshape(n - 4, 2)))

def optimize(n, initial):
    pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n)
             if j >= 4]
    ii = np.array([p[0] for p in pairs], dtype=int)
    jj = np.array([p[1] for p in pairs], dtype=int)
    m = len(pairs)

    p0 = np.vstack((SQUARE, initial))
    dv = p0[:, None, :] - p0[None, :, :]
    z0[-1] = max(2., float(np.max(np.sum(dv * dv, axis=2)))) + .1
    def constraints(z):
        p = make_points(z, n)
        d = p[ii] - p[jj]
        d2 = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", d, d)
        return np.r_[d2 - 1., z[-1] - d2]
    def constraint_jac(z):
        p = make_points(z, n)
        mat = np.zeros((2 * m, len(z)))
        for row, (i, j) in enumerate(pairs):
            grad = 2. * (p[i] - p[j])
            if i >= 4:
                mat[row, 2 * (i - 4):2 * (i - 4) + 2] = grad
            if j >= 4:
                mat[row, 2 * (j - 4):2 * (j - 4) + 2] = -grad
        mat[m:, :-1] = -mat[:m, :-1]
        mat[m:, -1] = 1.
        return mat
    obj_grad = np.r_[np.zeros(2 * (n - 4)), 1.]
    result = minimize(
        lambda z: z[-1], z0, jac=lambda z: obj_grad,
        method="SLSQP",
        constraints=[{"type": "ineq", "fun": constraints,
                      "jac": constraint_jac}],
        bounds=[(-6., 6.)] * (2 * (n - 4)) + [(2., 200.)],
        options={"maxiter": MAXITER, "ftol": 1e-10, "disp": False})

RESULT: An all-N non-circulant mixed-span theorem for a covering
three-component convex-thrackle forest.

Status: Complete analytic proof for an explicit infinite family.
It proves full mixed bar rank, not Erdos Problem #99.
No literature priority is claimed.

THEOREM

Let N >= 7 be an integer, and let P_1,...,P_N be the
counterclockwise vertices of a regular N-gon with unit sides.

Let C_N be its perimeter cycle and define

 E = {(1,v): 4 <= v <= N-2}
     union {(2,N-1),(3,N)}.

Then:

(1) E is a spanning convex-thrackle forest with exactly
    three connected components and N-3 edges.

(2) The planar infinitesimal rigidity matrix satisfies

       rank R(C_N union E) = 2N-3.

(3) Consequently, these N+(N-3) bars admit no nonzero
    equilibrium self-stress, even with unrestricted signs.

The result holds for every N >= 7, hence in particular for
every odd N >= 7. It is not an all-longest-chord result.

PROOF

1. Combinatorial structure.

The first component is the star centered at vertex 1,
with leaves 4,...,N-2. The remaining components are the
single edges (2,N-1) and (3,N).

All N vertices are covered, and the edge count is

       (N-5)+2 = N-3.

Every star edge meets every other star edge at vertex 1.

For 4 <= v <= N-2, the cyclic inequalities

       1 < 2 < v < N-1
       1 < 3 < v < N

show that (1,v) crosses each of the other two edges.
Finally,

       2 < 3 < N-1 < N

shows that (2,N-1) crosses (3,N).

Thus every two edges meet, either at an endpoint or
at an interior crossing. E is a convex thrackle.

Its three components are trees, so E is a forest.

2. Independent derivation of the mixed-span reduction.

Put

       t = pi/N,
       s_a = sin(a*t).

The N-1 successive perimeter bars form an independent
set of rigidity rows.

On their infinitesimal-motion kernel, write

       V_{i+1}-V_i = a_i J(P_{i+1}-P_i),

where J is counterclockwise rotation through 90 degrees.

Introduce the N-2 angular differences

       q_j = a_j-a_{j-1},  2 <= j <= N-1.
